procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 30.05.2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in BA No.1097 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi at New Delhi issued a Judgment and Order on 30.05.2023 in BA No.1097 of 2023. This appears to be a bail application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed to the Supreme Court from the High Court's order. The Supreme Court considered the assurance from the prosecution that the trial would be concluded in 6-8 months. The Supreme Court granted liberty to the appellant to move a fresh bail application if circumstances change or if the trial is unduly delayed.

directions: The observations made in this judgment, either way, are only for disposal of the present appeals, and these would not inﬂuence the trial court on the merits of the case, which would proceed in accordance with law, and decided on the basis of the evidence led.
All disputed factual and legal issues are left open.

issue.issue_text: Whether the right to bail due to a protracted trial, not attributable to the accused, should be read into Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and Section 45 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002.

facts: The case involved an accused person who had been incarcerated for a prolonged period during the trial.
The trial was protracted, and it was not clear that it would be decided within a foreseeable time.
The delay in the trial was not attributable to the accused.
The prosecution had given assurances that the trial would conclude, but it had not.

law.name: Article 21 of the Constitution of India
law.description: This article guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which has been interpreted to include the fundamental right to a speedy trial.

law.name: Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC)
law.description: This section provides special powers to the High Court or Court of Session regarding bail.

law.name: Section 45 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)
law.description: This section imposes stringent twin conditions for the grant of bail in money-laundering cases.

law.name: Section 436A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC)
law.description: This section provides for the release of an undertrial prisoner who has been detained for up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for the offense. The Court clarified this is not a mandatory minimum period one must serve before getting bail on grounds of delay.

application: The Supreme Court began with the principle that the constitutional mandate for a speedy trial is a 'higher law' that overrides statutory limitations.

It reasoned that pre-trial detention should not become a form of punishment. When a trial is delayed indefinitely for reasons not caused by the accused, continued incarceration amounts to punishment without a conviction.

The Court balanced the seriousness of the economic offense against the fundamental right to liberty. It distinguished the case from more heinous crimes (like murder, rape, or offenses under the NDPS Act) and cases involving thousands of defrauded depositors, suggesting that while the offense is serious, it does not automatically justify indefinite detention.

Based on the supremacy of the constitutional right to a speedy trial, the Court held that the 'right to bail in cases of delay, coupled with incarceration for a long period' must be read into both Section 439 of the CrPC and the stricter Section 45 of the PMLA.

Therefore, if a trial is protracted and not proceeding for reasons not attributable to the accused, the court is justified in exercising its power to grant bail, especially when the trial is expected to take years.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that the fundamental right to a speedy trial, as guaranteed by the Constitution, requires that the right to be granted bail due to a protracted trial (where the delay is not caused by the accused) must be read into the bail provisions of both Section 439 of the CrPC and Section 45 of the PMLA. This is because pre-trial detention cannot be allowed to become a punishment in itself.

issue.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of granting bail, economic offences should be equated with heinous crimes punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or long-term sentences like those under the NDPS Act, murder, or rape.

law.law_text: The right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution.
Detention or jail before being pronounced guilty of an offence should not become punishment without trial.
The right to bail in cases of trial delay, coupled with long incarceration, should be read into Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Section 45 of the PML Act.
Precedent from cases like P. Chidambaram v. Directorate of Enforcement establishes that even in cases of grave economic offence, it is not a rule that bail should be denied in every case.

application.application_text: The Court explicitly stated that it is "not proper to equate" economic offences with heinous crimes like murder, rape, or those under the NDPS Act, which are punishable with death, life imprisonment, or other long-term sentences.

The Court reasoned that when a trial is protracted for reasons not attributable to the accused, the constitutional right to a speedy trial becomes a significant factor. In such situations, the prayer for bail becomes meritorious.

The Court emphasized that prolonged pre-trial incarceration infringes on the fundamental right to life and liberty. Therefore, unless there are compelling reasons, a court should be guided to grant bail when a trial is not proceeding and is likely to take years.

The Court also noted that bail considerations must be made on a case-by-case basis, and in this specific instance, the case did not involve the defrauding of thousands of depositors, distinguishing it from certain other large-scale economic offences.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that economic offences should be equated with heinous crimes for bail purposes. It held that doing so would be improper, as it overlooks the fundamental right to a speedy trial and the principle that pre-trial detention should not become a punishment. The Court prioritized constitutional mandates and ruled that prolonged incarceration due to trial delays can be a meritorious ground for granting bail, even in economic offence cases.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 45 of the PML Act requires a court to arrive at a positive finding that the applicant has not committed an offence to grant bail, rather than a tentative finding based on broad probabilities.

law.law_name: Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PML Act)
law.description: This section outlines the conditions for granting bail for offences under the PML Act.
A Supreme Court judgment that interpreted the requirements for bail under Section 45 of the PML Act.

application.description: The Supreme Court, referring to its earlier decision in *Vijay Madanlal Choudhary*, held that Section 45 of the PML Act does not require a court to reach a 'positive finding' that the applicant has not committed an offence in order to grant bail.

The Court reasoned that Section 45 must be construed reasonably. It stated that the legislature's intent could not have been to require a court to conduct a detailed, threadbare examination of the case at the bail stage to pronounce a final verdict of guilt or acquittal.
It was noted that bail applications are typically decided long before the trial concludes, and sometimes even before it begins, making a definitive finding of innocence impractical.

Instead of a positive finding, the Court clarified that the correct standard for a bail application is to record a 'tentative finding' based on 'broad probabilities'. This involves an application of mind without meticulously weighing all the evidence as would be done in a full trial.
The Court also affirmed that any such tentative findings made for the purpose of granting or refusing bail will not have any bearing on the final merits of the case at trial.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that Section 45 of the PML Act requires a positive finding of innocence for bail. It concluded that a court only needs to arrive at a tentative finding based on broad probabilities that the accused has not committed the offence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the right to bail due to a protracted trial, not attributable to the accused, should be read into Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and Section 45 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that if a trial is protracted for an extended period without the fault of the accused, it violates their right to a speedy trial, and therefore, they should be granted bail even under the stringent conditions of the PMLA.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (prosecution) countered this by giving an assurance to the court that they would conclude the trial within the next six to eight months, implying that bail on the grounds of delay was not yet necessary.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of granting bail, economic offences should be equated with heinous crimes punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or long-term sentences like those under the NDPS Act, murder, or rape.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that economic offences should not be treated with the same severity as heinous crimes like murder or rape when considering bail, suggesting a less stringent approach should be adopted.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that economic offences are a grave class of crime that deeply impacts the financial health and sovereignty of the country and should be treated with the same seriousness as other heinous crimes, justifying strict bail conditions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 45 of the PML Act requires a court to arrive at a positive finding that the applicant has not committed an offence to grant bail, rather than a tentative finding based on broad probabilities.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that for granting bail under Section 45 of the PMLA, the court is only required to form a tentative opinion based on broad probabilities, not a positive and definitive finding that the accused has not committed the offence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that Section 45 imposes twin conditions that require a higher standard of satisfaction from the court, which is more than a mere tentative finding and closer to a positive satisfaction that the accused is not guilty, as upheld in the Vijay Madanlal Choudhary case.

cases.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Others v. Union of India and Other
cases.principle: In reference to Section 45 of the PML Act.

cases.case_name: Y. Balaji v. Karthik Desari and Another
cases.principle: For examining the contours of Section 3 of the PML Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional right to a speedy trial must be read into bail provisions, including Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Section 45 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002. When a trial is not proceeding for reasons not attributable to the accused, and it is clear the case will not be decided within a foreseeable time, a court may grant bail, as prolonged pre-trial incarceration should not become a punishment.
obiter: Rule of law means that laws apply equally to all citizens and institutions, including the State.
Rule of law requires an equal right to access to justice for the marginalised.
The rule also mandates objective and fair treatment to all.
Rule of law is a check on arbitrary use of powers.

While the prosecution may pertain to an economic oﬀence, yet it may not be proper to equate these cases with those punishable with death, imprisonment for life, ten years or more like oﬀences under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, murder, cases of rape, dacoity, kidnaping for ransom, mass violence, etc.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the Court accepted in principle that the constitutional right to a speedy trial requires that bail can be granted for protracted delays even under the stringent PMLA, and that economic offences should not be equated with heinous crimes like murder, it ultimately denied bail at this stage. The denial was based on specific, undisputed evidence presented by the prosecution showing proceeds of crime amounting to ₹338 crores, which prevented the court from forming the tentative opinion required to satisfy the twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the mandate from Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (supra), which requires an examination of allegations to form a tentative opinion regarding the twin conditions under Section 45 of the PML Act for the grant of bail.

The court established that the right to bail due to a protracted trial, not attributable to the accused, should be read into Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Section 45 of the PML Act, as the constitutional mandate for a speedy trial is the higher law.
why_appellant_lost: The Court was not inclined to grant bail at this stage because the prosecution presented a figure of ₹338 crores as excess commission earned by wholesale distributors in ten months, which it considered proceeds of crime, and noted that this figure "cannot be disputed or challenged" at the bail hearing.
This evidence prevented the appellant from satisfying the stringent twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA, as the court could not form a tentative opinion that he was not guilty.

Although the court accepted the principle of bail for trial delay, it was not applied because the prosecution had given an assurance to conclude the trial within a foreseeable time, making the argument premature.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully presented evidence of proceeds of crime amounting to ₹338 crores, which the court found compelling enough at the bail stage to establish a prima facie case.
The respondent's arguments relied on the stringent twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA, as upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary, which the court applied to the facts of the case.
The respondent's assurance to conclude the trial in the near future effectively countered the appellant's argument for bail on the grounds of delay, at least for the time being.
policy_considerations: Detention or jail before being pronounced guilty of an offence should not become punishment without trial.

The constitutional mandate for a speedy trial is a higher law and a basic right of the accused, which should be read into bail provisions, including Section 45 of the PMLA, especially when the trial is not proceeding for reasons not attributable to the accused.

It may not be proper to equate economic offences with heinous crimes punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or long-term sentences like those under the NDPS Act, murder, or rape, particularly when the case does not involve the defrauding of thousands of depositors.
